#### Before you send your drawing

Can I submit an incomplete drawing? Yes. Mark the unresolved details and describe the application. Feasibility and pricing depend on confirming the final requirements.

Are material and finish options pre-approved? No. Available options must be confirmed for your actual part. Read our material selection guide for the information to prepare.

#### Start with the interface a standard screw cannot satisfy

Use this route when the requirement combines features or does not fit a single product family. Identify the reason for customization: inaccessible drive, unusual bearing face, mixed threads, internal passage or several locating steps. Separate essential interfaces from dimensions that can be discussed during manufacturability review.

#### Turn an early concept into a controlled specification

Send a drawing with units and revision, or a sample with a dimensioned sketch. Identify unresolved requirements explicitly. A sample is useful for understanding shape, but cannot establish the original alloy, heat treatment, hidden tolerances or approval criteria. Agree those requirements before treating a sample as a production specification.

#### Compare the complete manufacturing proposal

Review tooling, forming or turning, secondary features, thread generation, treatment and final checks together. A low initial forming cost may be offset by additional finishing, while a machined prototype may not represent the preferred repeat-production route. Compare sample and recurring order quantities using the same approved specification.

#### From drawing to approved samples

Provide the drawing, material, finish and intended assembly. Identify the drawing revision, prototype quantity and expected repeat demand. Where the first part is based on an existing sample, separately confirm material and hidden features rather than inferring them from appearance.

The typical sampling lead time, including tooling, is approximately 10–15 days. The schedule is confirmed after drawing review and agreement on the sample specification; material availability, special treatment and inspection requirements can affect the confirmed date. Confirm when the agreed schedule starts in the quotation. Sample approval and repeat-production delivery are separate milestones.

#### Common specification questions

Can the shoulder and thread have different diameters? Yes, the shoulder and thread are specified independently. Review the transition, available mating clearance and effective thread engagement as one geometry.

Is every shoulder screw ground? No. The final size, form and surface requirements determine the finishing route. Review the need for grinding with treatment distortion and the final acceptance condition.

#### Follow a complete application design

Explore a proposed assembly, the fastener choices, manufacturing review and sample validation plan. This is an illustrative design study, with no claimed customer delivery or measured performance.

Review the fixture shoulder and axial-stack concept ↗

#### Choose the shoulder around its actual function

A locating shoulder, a rotating pivot and a spacing stop impose different requirements. For a pivot, examine the mating bore, running clearance and contact length. For a spacer, the shoulder length controls the clamped stack. For a locating feature, identify the datum axis and the surfaces that establish position. A close diameter tolerance alone does not resolve these different functions.

#### Check the axial stack before tightening

Consider a cover rotating on a shoulder screw. If the shoulder ends below the cover stack, tightening may clamp the moving part. If it projects too far, excessive axial play can remain. Show the complete stack, washers and seating face on the assembly drawing; then dimension the shoulder length against the intended clearance rather than copying the overall screw length. This is an illustrative design review, not a released customer design.

#### Protect the transition and final fit

The shoulder-to-thread transition needs enough clearance for the mating part to seat. Specify usable thread engagement separately from the visible threaded length and show any relief. Review straightness, runout and surface texture where these affect motion. If heat treatment or coating follows machining, establish which shoulder dimensions are accepted in the final supplied condition and whether finishing allowance is needed.

#### Select the route and verify the result

CNC turning is a route to review for sample quantities and complex steps. Cold heading followed by local machining can be evaluated for repeat production. Grinding is selected where size, form or surface requirements justify it, rather than assumed from the product name. CCD inspection can screen accessible profiles; datum relationships, surface texture and thread acceptance need their own suitable methods.

#### Review the route before fixing the quotation

For shoulder & step screws, review Cold Heading + Secondary Machining, Swiss-Type & CNC Turning, Secondary & Precision Operations against the drawing and quantity. Identify which features can be produced in the initial shape and which require a separate setup. A change to a functional shoulder, bore, drive or thread can change the proposed route as well as the inspection effort.

The drawing review should resolve shoulder diameter & length; thread & transition; precision options. Keep material condition and finishing allowance attached to those requirements. Define the acceptance condition for critical features and approve any proposed dimensional change before comparing samples with the original assembly.

#### From drawing to approved samples

Include mating bore details, critical shoulder dimensions, surface texture and required dimensional inspection. Identify the drawing revision, prototype quantity and expected repeat demand. Where the first part is based on an existing sample, separately confirm material and hidden features rather than inferring them from appearance.

ENGINEERING GUIDE

##### How to prepare an inspection plan for custom screws ↗

An inspection plan translates a drawing into agreed checks and records. Define it during the quotation stage so acceptance is understood before production.

#### How is a shoulder screw different from a fully threaded bolt?

A shoulder screw has an unthreaded bearing or locating section between its head and thread. Select that shoulder for the required rotation, location or spacing function, and specify thread engagement separately. A fully threaded bolt does not provide the same smooth bearing surface.

#### How do I choose the shoulder length without clamping a moving part?

Review the complete axial stack, including washers and the mating seat. The shoulder must seat as intended while preserving the specified movement clearance. Show the assembly and tolerance stack on the drawing; nominal shoulder length alone cannot establish the final clearance.

CCD Vision & Dimensional Inspection

#### Dimensions & geometry

Review the relevant process ↗

Material evidence, specified HV/HRC hardness, strength and heat-treatment documentation.

Review the relevant process ↗

Review the relevant process ↗

Torque, tensile, fatigue, metallography or hydrogen evaluation where the application calls for them.

Review the relevant process ↗

Drawing revision, agreed sampling, first-article/sample approval, traceability and requested reports.

Review the relevant process ↗

Agree which features need 100% screening and which use an approved sampling plan. Full dimensional screening does not replace material or destructive test requirements.

### What to include in a custom screw RFQ

A useful quotation starts with a clear specification. A drawing is the best starting point, but a sample, sketch or assembly description can also help define the next questions.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026 Custom Metal Screws

IN THIS GUIDE Start with the drawing and revision Identify the features that matter Specify material and finish separately Include quantity and delivery context Your RFQ checklist Separate mandatory requirements from discussion items Use a quotation comparison sheet Close the review with a release decision RELATED PRODUCT Custom Metal Screws ↗

#### Start with the drawing and revision

Include the drawing number, revision, units and quantity. Show overall length, thread specification, head dimensions and any shoulders. If a requirement is still open, label it as open rather than leaving it ambiguous.

#### Identify the features that matter

Mark dimensions that affect fit or function. Explain the mating part, assembly access and service conditions. A tolerance on every surface may create unnecessary cost; let functional needs guide the discussion.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom metal screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

#### Specify material and finish separately

State a material grade if it is known. Identify any coating, appearance or corrosion requirements separately. A material family or a finish name alone may not be enough to define an acceptance requirement.

#### Include quantity and delivery context

Provide prototype quantity, initial order quantity and expected repeat demand if available. Include the destination and requested date. Lead time and feasibility need confirmation after technical review.

#### Your RFQ checklist

Drawing or sketch • revision and units • material • finish • critical features • quantity • inspection documents • destination. Downloading a checklist is optional: you can paste these details directly into the quotation form.

#### Separate mandatory requirements from discussion items

Mark the interfaces that must remain unchanged: mating thread, locating diameter, bearing face and available installation envelope. Identify other features as open for review where that is true. A supplier can then propose a manufacturing change without silently changing the assembly function. If a drawing note conflicts with a model or sample, record the controlling requirement before obtaining a production quotation.

#### Use a quotation comparison sheet

Compare the same drawing revision and quantities. List one-time tooling, samples, recurring parts, treatment, inspection records, packaging and delivery terms separately. Ask each proposal to identify exclusions and deviations. A price for a blank that excludes a critical finishing operation is not equivalent to a price for an accepted finished part.

#### Close the review with a release decision

The quotation review should end with an agreed specification, confirmed sample quantity, schedule basis and acceptance plan. Typical tooling and sampling is approximately 10–15 days, subject to review. Repeat-production delivery is separate. Keep unresolved points visible so an early commercial estimate is not mistaken for an approved manufacturing release.

Ready to discuss your part? Use the RFQ preparation checklist , then submit your drawing for review . For acceptance requirements, see quality planning .

General guidance only. Material properties, tolerances, standards and manufacturing feasibility must be verified for the actual specification. This article does not establish a product performance guarantee.

### A practical guide to shoulder screw drawings

The shoulder, thread and head work together as one geometry. A clear drawing explains not only the dimensions, but also which surfaces locate, rotate or clamp in your assembly.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026 Shoulder & Step Screws

IN THIS GUIDE Define the shoulder Show how the thread ends Review head access and seating Communicate functional tolerances Draw the assembly stack, not only the screw Choose datums that match the locating function Approve the final supplied surface RELATED PRODUCT Shoulder & Step Screws ↗

#### Define the shoulder

Dimension shoulder diameter and shoulder length independently from thread length. Explain whether the shoulder serves as a locating surface, bearing surface or spacer. The functional role helps identify which features need closer review.

#### Show how the thread ends

State thread designation and length, and show any relief or transition at the shoulder. Check how the screw seats in the mating assembly. Do not assume the end of the usable thread is identical to the end of the visible thread form.

Working on this type of part? Explore our shoulder & step screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

#### Review head access and seating

Include head diameter, height and drive configuration. Consider the tool clearance and seating surface in the assembly. A head that fits the drawing may still be inaccessible once neighboring parts are installed.

#### Communicate functional tolerances

Mark the mating bore relationship and any surface finish requirement that affects motion or fit. Tolerances should be established by the application engineer and confirmed during manufacturing review.

#### Draw the assembly stack, not only the screw

Show the seating face, moving component, washer or bushing and intended axial clearance. Dimension the shoulder length against this stack. If the shoulder is too short, tightening can clamp the moving part; too long can leave excessive movement. Review the worst permitted stack before approving shoulder length, rather than adjusting it after a binding prototype is received.

#### Choose datums that match the locating function

Identify the axis and face that locate the part in service. Decide whether shoulder form, runout or another specified relationship affects the mechanism. Listing only outside diameters can leave the functional relationship undefined. Agree how the relationship is checked, particularly if the part is located differently during successive machining operations.

#### Approve the final supplied surface

Treatment and coating may change the condition used to accept the shoulder. State final limits and coating coverage on the functional surface. The inspection record should distinguish shoulder measurement from thread gauging. A correct thread does not establish that the pivot fits, and a correct external silhouette does not establish surface texture.

A high-strength steel fastener needs a coating decision that considers both corrosion and hydrogen exposure throughout processing.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026 Material-Specific Heat Treatment

#### Identify the susceptible condition

Strength, hardness, material condition and tensile stress influence susceptibility. Cleaning, pickling and electroplating can be hydrogen sources. Property class alone is not a complete risk assessment.

#### Define a coating system

Specify the substrate, process, coating thickness, friction and acceptance requirements. Zinc-flake deposition can avoid electrolytic deposition, but pretreatment and other steps must still be reviewed.

Working on this type of part? Explore our shoulder & step screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

#### Understand the limit of baking

Hydrogen-relief baking can reduce risk under a controlled specification. It is not a guarantee that every fastener is free from embrittlement. Define any required process controls and verification with the responsible technical team.

#### Write a useful RFQ

Include grade, final properties, coating specification, functional fits, documentation and application requirements. Avoid a blanket rule that every zinc finish is forbidden or that every coating requires the same baking cycle.

#### Map potential exposure through the full route

Review cleaning and pretreatment alongside deposition. A non-electrolytic coating does not remove every possible hydrogen source elsewhere in the sequence. Relate the process to the specified material condition and application stress. Avoid treating either a coating trade name or a property-class label as a complete risk assessment.

#### Define evidence before the order

The responsible technical review should establish the applicable process controls, any relief requirement, verification and records. A generic statement that parts were baked omits the conditions that made the process applicable. Risk reduction is not a guarantee of elimination; decide the acceptance scope under the actual specification rather than substituting a blanket zinc ban or blanket bake instruction.

#### Keep corrosion, friction and fit in the same review

Changing a coating to address one concern can alter thread allowance, friction or the bearing surface. Reassess the assembly and dimensional requirements when the surface system changes. A corrosion test result under stated conditions does not prove field life or the absence of embrittlement. These are different acceptance questions.

By Theo Wan • ZUFEK Technical Editorial • Published October 29, 2026 Material-Specific Heat Treatment

IN THIS GUIDE Distinguish austenitic from precipitation-hardening grades State the purpose of solution treatment Define the final condition of 17-4PH Coordinate finish and verification Resolve what the drawing means by high-strength stainless Separate material treatment from surface treatment Review assembly galling as a separate mechanism RELATED PRODUCT Custom Metal Screws ↗

#### Distinguish austenitic from precipitation-hardening grades

304 and 316 are austenitic stainless steels and are not hardened by the precipitation-aging treatment used for 17-4PH. They can strengthen through cold work, which must be considered separately from heat treatment.

#### State the purpose of solution treatment

Solution annealing and stress-related treatments have material-specific purposes and can affect corrosion behavior and dimensional condition. They should not be treated as a universal hardening cycle.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom metal screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

#### Define the final condition of 17-4PH

A precipitation-hardening grade requires an explicitly selected condition and corresponding property requirements. Do not assume that any aging cycle is interchangeable with another.

#### Coordinate finish and verification

Passivation is a surface treatment, not the same operation as solution treatment or precipitation hardening. State material evidence, final properties, critical dimensions and requested inspection records.

#### Resolve what the drawing means by high-strength stainless

Clarify whether the requirement names a finished fastener class or a specific alloy and condition. A change from an austenitic grade to 17-4PH changes the material specification as well as the treatment discussion. It needs approval against corrosion, mechanical and application requirements; it is not a manufacturing shortcut to apply without the designer.

#### Separate material treatment from surface treatment

Passivation addresses surface condition; it is not a replacement for the specified material condition. Keep material evidence, mechanical requirements and the surface process separately identifiable in the order. A visually similar surface does not prove that the correct alloy or final condition was supplied.

#### Review assembly galling as a separate mechanism

A selected stainless grade does not eliminate the need to review thread contact and the mating pair. Surface condition, assembly and lubrication can affect galling, and a lubrication change can also affect tightening behavior. Coordinate the assembly process with the approved specification instead of using an unqualified torque figure from another joint.

A tightening instruction belongs to the joint, not just the screw diameter. Friction, bearing conditions and the assembly method influence the relationship between tightening torque and clamp load.

#### Describe the complete joint

Provide the mating thread, clamped stack, bearing surfaces and intended function. Include washers, inserts and other components that affect assembly. A torque copied from an unrelated table may have assumptions that do not match this connection.

#### Identify the friction condition

Coating, lubrication and contact surfaces can change tightening behavior. State the supplied and assembly conditions that the design uses. Do not change a lubricant or finish solely for appearance without reviewing whether the existing tightening instruction remains appropriate.

#### Distinguish reference values from validation

Reference torque information can support an engineering discussion but is not a substitute for evaluating a specific joint. Agree the responsible design calculation, test or approval process. Document the tool method, acceptance criteria and any required checks with the approved part specification. If the screw or surface system changes, consider whether the assembly instruction needs review. #### Specification example

Replacing a plain screw with an integral flange changes the bearing interface. Review the joint assumptions before carrying over the original torque instruction solely because the nominal thread is unchanged.

Packaging is part of the delivered condition. It should protect functional surfaces, preserve identification and make the incoming inspection and assembly process practical.

Consider exposed threads, precision shoulders, applied locking material and any cleaned internal passage. State special protection requirements rather than assuming bulk packing is suitable for every part. The supplier needs to know which handling damage or contamination would make the component unacceptable.

#### Define quantities and identification

Agree pack quantity, part number, drawing revision and lot information required on the label. Avoid introducing unapproved markings on the component itself to solve a packaging identification issue.

Working on this type of part? Explore our custom metal screws and include the functional requirements in your RFQ.

#### Coordinate cleanliness and preservation

Protective oil, corrosion prevention and clean packaging serve different needs and can conflict. Specify permitted residues and the expected condition at delivery. #### Connect the lot to the records

Define which inspection or material documents accompany the shipment and how they relate to the identified lot. Keep the traceability requirement proportionate to the actual order. A label containing a batch number is only useful when the agreed records can be associated with that number.

#### Specification example

For two nearly identical shoulder lengths, use separate clearly labeled packages and the correct part references. A shared bulk bag can defeat otherwise careful dimensional inspection by creating an avoidable assembly mix-up.

### Thread Rolling, Cutting & Tapping

The thread profile, material and batch conditions determine whether rolling, cutting, grinding or an internal tapping process is appropriate.

Thread Rolling, Cutting & Tapping

#### Flat-die and cylindrical-die rolling

External threads are formed by displacement. Suitable material condition, blank diameter and tool geometry are essential. Machine capability sets the actual size range; no universal M0.8–M12 limit applies.

#### Single-point cutting and special profiles

Turning can address specified pitches, tapers and special profiles where tooling and access permit. NPT, MJ and other named threads require the applicable complete specification, not an approximate profile.

#### Internal cut and form tapping

Cut tapping removes material; form tapping displaces a sufficiently ductile material and needs the correct pre-hole. Neither method is universally stronger in every grade and geometry.

#### Acceptance and sequence

Define designation, class, usable length, runout and gauging. Rolling may improve fatigue behavior in suitable conditions, but is not a blanket strength guarantee. Review whether threading occurs before or after heat treatment.

### Material-Specific Heat Treatment

Heat-treatment selection follows the alloy, required condition and applicable acceptance specification. One sequence cannot be applied to every screw.

#### Quench and temper

Suitable carbon and alloy steels can be processed to specified mechanical requirements. Property classes such as 8.8, 10.9 and 12.9 require an applicable specification and verification; treatment names alone do not establish the class.

Carburizing and hardening can produce a hardened surface with a different core condition. A grade such as 10B21 does not by itself prescribe carburizing: specify core properties, case requirements and application.

#### Stainless and titanium distinctions

304/316 austenitic stainless steels are not precipitation-hardening grades. Solution annealing serves a different purpose from aging 17-4PH. Titanium and other alloys need grade-specific treatment; do not transfer a stainless cycle to them.

#### Stress relief and stability

Stress-relief or specialist cryogenic treatments are selected only where justified by material condition and dimensional needs. State the required final condition and review distortion, corrosion and finish compatibility.

### CCD Vision & Dimensional Inspection

Non-contact optical checks for screw length, head diameter and visible stepped profiles, combined with the gauges and tests required by the drawing.

CCD Vision & Dimensional Inspection

#### CCD optical dimension checks

Camera-based vision measurement uses suitable optics, lighting and calibrated edge detection to check accessible external dimensions such as overall length, head diameter and shoulder profile. A stable presentation and validated inspection program are needed for the specified part.

#### Complementary verification

Silhouette inspection does not establish internal geometry, material strength or every thread characteristic. Use the specified thread gauges, additional dimensional methods and functional tests where required. Agree acceptance criteria and the actual inspection coverage.

#### Material and mechanical checks

Material documentation, HV/HRC hardness, tensile, torque or destructive testing are selected when applicable. A test name needs a method, sample quantity and acceptance criterion.

#### Surface and specialist checks

Coating thickness, specified salt-spray testing, metallography, fatigue and hydrogen-embrittlement evaluation require an agreed scope. Salt spray results do not directly predict service life.

#### Sampling versus full inspection

Agree which characteristics receive 100% screening, sampling or first-article approval. Equipment availability, external laboratory work and reporting are confirmed for the order; no unverified in-house laboratory claim is made.

MATERIAL SELECTION WORKFLOW

### Grade, condition and joint. Make the choice together.

A material name is the beginning of a specification. The required finished properties, environment and assembly determine whether it is suitable.

#### 1. State the function before the alloy

Separate the load-bearing function from locating, adjustment, electrical contact or a passage. State the environment, mating metals and cleaning conditions. A screw used for an optical adjuster may have a different priority from a clamp in an outdoor housing, even when the outline looks similar.

#### 2. Keep strength values attached to their basis

Identify whether the quoted number describes stock material or a finished fastener class. Record grade, temper or heat-treatment condition, product form and the applicable specification. Do not transfer a stock tensile figure directly to the assembled load capacity. Thread engagement and the mating component can govern the connection.

Requirement Route to investigate Question to resolve

Specified steel fastener property class Carbon/alloy steel or suitable 10B21 route Which material and final condition meet the ordered class and verification?

Corrosion exposure with a stainless preference SUS304 / SUS316 and the applicable finished requirement Which environment, mating metals, strength and galling controls apply?

Low mass with a machined shape Named aluminum alloy and temper; titanium only where justified What thread engagement, wear and surface conditions are required?

Electrical or thermal contact A specified copper grade; brass only where appropriate What conductivity, contact finish and mechanical acceptance are needed?

Adjustment and custom turned details A grade-specific steel, stainless or brass option How do wear, contact, thread fit and manufacturing economics compare?

#### 3. Review surface and assembly effects

A coating can alter dimensions and friction. Stainless, titanium and other combinations may need an assembly-specific galling review. Lubrication or a coating change must be coordinated with the assembly process rather than added after a torque requirement has been agreed. High-strength steel surface processing also needs a hydrogen-risk assessment for the actual route.

#### 4. Approve evidence and changes

Specify material documentation, final mechanical requirements, dimensional acceptance and any coating or functional checks needed for the order. Agree who approves an alternate grade or condition. Sample approval should identify the exact material and process revision so a later substitution is visible.

#### Illustrative comparison

For a screw retaining an outdoor cover, compare a specified stainless solution with a coated-steel solution against the same environment, joint requirements and acceptance plan. Do not select solely from color or a single nominal strength number. The review should resolve corrosion, engagement, friction, visible condition and required records before a final quotation.

Custom flange screw retaining a module cover on a tapped boss The flange bears on the cover. Usable thread engagement and blind-hole depth are reviewed together so the screw seats before bottoming. Flange bearing face Cover Thread engagement Bottom clearance Service access, material and surface system need joint-level review.

Concept status Proposed design study. No customer delivery, performance result or certification is claimed. Dimensions, loads and final acceptance require approval for the actual assembly.

#### Project brief and system boundary

Design a custom screw concept for a serviceable automotive electronic-module cover fixed to a threaded housing. The proposed role is cover retention and controlled seating. The fastener is not assigned a crash, battery containment, electrical bonding or pressure-sealing function in this study. Any such requirement would change the design and approval scope. The study is a proposed engineering workflow, not an account of a delivered Mercedes-Benz, BMW or other customer project.

#### Assembly assumptions to confirm

Assume a cover with defined clearance holes, a housing with tapped bosses and restricted space around the screw head. The actual cover material, housing alloy, boss depth, gasket arrangement, external exposure and service access remain inputs to be confirmed. No screw diameter, tightening torque or strength class is released from these assumptions. Obtain a section through the joint and the cover stack before choosing dimensions.

#### Choose the fastener structure

Investigate an integral flange screw to reduce separately handled hardware and provide a defined bearing footprint. Compare the flange diameter and under-head radius with the cover hole, boss and nearby walls. Begin with a plain bearing face if appearance or cover marking is a concern; a serrated face requires a separate contact review. A special drive is an option only if restricted service access is a requirement. Confirm that the authorized tool can reach and fully engage the recess.

#### Resolve engagement and bottoming

Dimension the under-head stack and usable thread against the tapped boss. Verify that the screw seats on the intended bearing surface before the tip reaches the bottom of a blind hole. Define usable thread, lead-in and any unthreaded transition separately. If a gasket is present, its compression and the joint clamp requirement belong to the enclosure design; this study does not claim that a flange screw creates a seal.

#### Compare material and surface options

Compare a specified coated-steel proposal with a grade- and condition-defined stainless proposal where appropriate. Use the same mechanical, exposure and assembly requirements for both. For steel, select the final properties together with heat treatment and the complete coating route, including hydrogen-risk controls where applicable. For stainless, review the required finished properties, mating metals and galling. Do not pick a finish solely because a different assembly passed a salt-spray test.

#### Prototype and production route

For an early geometry or limited samples, review a turned or otherwise suitable sample route. For repeated production, evaluate cold heading of the head and flange, the selected thread-generation stage and any secondary operation needed for the drive or local features. Include treatment, coating, cleaning and final inspection in the proposal. Record if the sample route differs from production, and decide which features or properties need confirmation on production-route samples.

#### Risk and validation plan

Risks include flange interference, cover marking, insufficient engagement, blind-hole bottoming, inadequate tool access, coating-related fit changes and an unsuitable assembly friction condition. Inspect the finished flange envelope and head geometry, gauge the specified thread and check installation in representative mating parts. Agree material and surface evidence separately. Any torque, clamp-load, corrosion or vibration evaluation needs a defined method, conditions and acceptance criteria; this study supplies no pass result.

#### Tooling, samples and release gates

Gate 1: confirm joint requirements and drawing revision. Gate 2: agree the proposed route, one-time tooling, sample quantity and acceptance plan. Typical sampling including tooling is approximately 10–15 days, with the schedule basis and exceptions confirmed in the quotation. Gate 3: inspect finished samples and trial the intended assembly/tool. Gate 4: approve or revise the drawing and process before releasing a repeat-production order. Production delivery is quoted separately.

#### Repeat-order control and handover

The release package should identify the approved screw drawing, material/final condition, surface specification, mating assembly revision, sample decisions, inspection scope and packaging/lot identification. Reassess changes to the housing, cover thickness, coating or driver. A confirmed automotive supply-chain background is company context, not evidence that this proposed enclosure design is OEM-approved.

#### What remains open

The customer must establish the loads, service temperature, exposure, thread dimensions and engagement, torque or other assembly-control method, required tests and release authority. Final feasibility and quoted commitments follow that review. This prevents an illustrative concept from being mistaken for a validated production design.

An illustrative pivot-fixture project connecting shoulder fits, axial stack, adjustment, route selection, CCD limits and sample approval.

Application concept visualization · not a customer installation or dimensioned drawing

#### Assembly concept

The plain shoulder supports the moving plate; the threaded end retains the screw in the base. The separate adjuster acts on a stop surface. Schematic only, not to scale. The geometry is not a released drawing.

Shoulder screw pivot with a separate adjustment stop The plain shoulder supports the moving plate; the threaded end retains the screw in the base. The separate adjuster acts on a stop surface. Moving plate Plain shoulder Axial clearance Separate adjuster Mounting base Thread retention and locating fit are separate interfaces.

Concept status Proposed design study. No customer delivery, performance result or certification is claimed. Dimensions, loads and final acceptance require approval for the actual assembly.

#### Project brief and operating concept

Develop a serviceable pivot-and-stop concept for an automation fixture. A shoulder screw retains a moving plate and provides its defined pivot surface; a separate knurled adjuster establishes a stop position. Keeping the two functions distinct allows pivot clearance and adjustment contact to be reviewed independently. This is an illustrative proposed project, with no claimed customer installation, tested cycle life or achieved positioning accuracy.

#### Define interfaces before dimensions

Obtain the moving plate, mating bore, mounting base and any washers or bushings in an assembly section. Identify the locating datum, required movement, operating range, contact surfaces and available tool access. The mechanism designer must establish loads, allowable play, duty cycle, wear and any guarding requirements. The screw alone does not establish the safety or accuracy of the fixture.

#### Shoulder diameter and axial stack

Define shoulder diameter against the mating bore and intended clearance. Define shoulder length from the seating face so tightening the screw retains the plate without unintentionally clamping its motion. Include all parts in the axial stack and the intended clearance. An excessively short shoulder can clamp the plate; an excessively long shoulder can leave unintended axial movement. Review the actual tolerance stack before releasing limits.

#### Transition, thread and service access

Provide clearance for the shoulder-to-thread transition and define usable engagement in the base. Check whether the tip can bottom in a blind hole before the screw seats. Keep the head and driver accessible through the permitted movement and service sequence. The thread class controls the threaded interface; it is not a substitute for the tolerance on the plain locating shoulder.

#### Adjustment screw and retention of setting

Select the knurled head envelope around finger clearance. Define the contact end, mating stop surface and required travel. Pitch describes nominal movement per turn, while the mechanism, thread fit and contact affect the actual setting. Establish a separate locking arrangement where the application requires retention under its operating conditions. Do not treat a fine thread or hand grip as proof of repeatability or vibration resistance.

#### Material and finishing review

Compare an appropriate steel or stainless solution against wear, exposure, mating material and the required final condition. If a controlled shoulder surface is coated, define the finished size and coverage. If the material is treated after machining, review possible dimensional change and whether finishing is needed afterward. Grinding is a possible route for specified size, form or texture; it is not mandatory simply because the product is a shoulder screw.

#### Sample route and repeat production

Review CNC turning for the initial compound geometry and local thread/relief features. A repeat-production alternative may begin with a cold-headed blank followed by precision secondary work. Cost and feasibility should include all local features, treatment, final finishing and inspection. When samples and production use different routes, agree what must be reconfirmed before transferring the approved design.

#### Inspection and functional trial

Check shoulder size and length, seating geometry, specified datum relationships and thread acceptance in the final supplied condition. CCD screening can address accessible external profile dimensions after the setup is validated. Surface texture, internal geometry and some datum relationships need complementary methods. In the assembly trial, examine full movement, intended axial clearance, access to the adjuster, contact at the travel limits and retention of the setting under the agreed conditions.

#### Sample approval and change loop

Agree the drawing, material, route and inspection plan before tooling and samples. Typical sampling including tooling is approximately 10–15 days, subject to review and confirmation. Compare the sample report with the approved requirements and document the mating-part trial. If binding or excess movement is observed, investigate the stack, transition, bore and final surface condition before changing one dimension in isolation. Reinspect affected features after a revision.

#### Release package and open requirements

Retain the approved assembly section, screw and adjuster drawings, material/final condition, finish coverage, inspection methods and sample decisions. Set the real load, life, travel, play and positional acceptance with the machine designer; no numerical performance is claimed here. Record the revision that passed the agreed trial before ordering repeat parts, and re-evaluate changes to the plate, bore or surface system.

Industry Insights

### EV charging enclosures: why fastener specifications must follow the joint

The growth of electric mobility creates more equipment interfaces, but it does not create one universal electric-vehicle screw. A charging cabinet door, a power-module bracket and a cable-management cover have different jobs. A purchasing team that starts with a photograph and asks for an “EV-grade fastener” has skipped the decisions that determine whether the part can be manufactured, assembled and serviced consistently. The useful starting point is the joint: what is being held together, which surfaces make contact, what movement is permitted, and what evidence will demonstrate an acceptable result.

Theo Wan · 2026-10-30 What the industry evidence actually tells us Separate the enclosure functions before choosing the screw Treat the axial stack as a controlled interface Make the final finish part of the dimensional discussion Security features must remain serviceable Select the manufacturing route against the real order pattern An illustrative drawing-review exercise Build an acceptance plan that matches the failure modes Ask better purchasing questions A practical handover package

#### What the industry evidence actually tells us

The IEA Global EV Outlook 2026 examines electric-vehicle deployment and charging infrastructure. It is a useful source for understanding the direction and diversity of electrification projects. It is not a component approval, a drawing standard or evidence that a particular screw will meet an equipment requirement. This article uses that report as market context. The manufacturing and procurement discussion that follows is ZUFEK editorial analysis, not a finding attributed to the IEA.

Market expansion can increase the number of enclosure platforms and purchasing programmes that a supplier encounters. It can also increase pressure to share parts between product variants. Sharing a screw is attractive when it reduces inventory, but a common appearance does not establish a common functional requirement. A change in panel thickness, gasket design, coating or access direction can invalidate an apparently simple substitution. The engineering question is therefore not whether charging equipment needs more screws. It is how a buyer can preserve the intended interface while changing scale, configuration or supply source.

#### Separate the enclosure functions before choosing the screw

Start by identifying whether the screw clamps a static joint, controls a gap, locates a component, retains a removable cover or limits unauthorised access. These functions can coexist, but they should not be left implicit. A flange head distributes contact differently from a smaller bearing face. A shoulder can establish an assembly distance, but it can also prevent a gasket from reaching its intended compression if the stack is wrong. A security recess limits the tools that can engage the head; it does not itself provide a sealing system.

Write a short functional statement alongside the part drawing. For example: “Retain the removable outer cover against its defined seating features, using the approved service tool, without relying on the screw thread as a locating surface.” That statement still needs dimensions and validation, but it is more useful than “special screw for charger.” It tells the reviewer which features need attention and discourages a supplier from optimising only the loose part. Include the mating-part drawing or an assembly section when the function cannot be understood from the screw alone.

#### Treat the axial stack as a controlled interface

An enclosure joint may contain a formed panel, a gasket, a washer, a spacer and a threaded insert. Each contributes to the installed condition. The overall screw length is only one part of that stack. The usable thread engagement must be distinguished from the total length of visible thread, and available depth must be distinguished from usable depth. A blind receiving feature can create an apparently tight assembly when the screw is actually bottoming before the bearing face seats.

Show the intended seating surfaces and the condition in which measurements apply. If a gasket is involved, obtain its compression requirements from the equipment or gasket design authority. Do not infer them from a screw supplier’s catalogue. If the enclosure uses a shoulder to limit travel, review the shoulder length against both extremes of the assembly stack. The drawing review should identify whether the fastener is expected to clamp, stop or float. Those are different outcomes, and an inspection plan must be able to distinguish them.

#### Make the final finish part of the dimensional discussion

A coating decision can affect more than appearance. The buyer should identify which surfaces are coated, which interfaces are sensitive to added material, and which final dimensions will be accepted after treatment. A shoulder that locates in a close-fitting bore needs a different review from a generous clearance hole. A threaded feature also needs an agreed acceptance condition after the selected treatment. Asking for a surface finish after approving dimensions can create avoidable rework or an unreviewed change in fit.

Corrosion resistance, friction and material compatibility should be considered together with the installation environment. An outdoor location alone is not a complete exposure specification. Ask about sheltered versus exposed service, cleaning practices, contact with other materials and the equipment manufacturer’s validation requirements. A salt-spray result on a loose fastener is not a direct prediction of field life for the assembled enclosure. If a coating or material is changed, review the joint and the acceptance evidence rather than treating colour similarity as equivalence.

#### Security features must remain serviceable

A tamper-resistant drive is an interface between the head, the matching bit and the available access space. Define the exact recess geometry or a controlled reference, the tool that will be used, and whether the tool can approach the head in the assembled equipment. A centre pin, deep recess or unusual head profile may affect forming and inspection. A head that works on a bench can be difficult to use when a cable tray or cabinet wall restricts tool alignment.

Serviceability should be reviewed with the people who maintain the equipment. Identify whether the part will be removed repeatedly, whether dropping it into the enclosure would create a problem, and whether a captive design is appropriate. Captivity is an assembly function involving the panel or retention feature, not a property guaranteed by a screw’s name. Agree the intended retained movement and removal procedure. Do not claim that a special drive is theft-proof or that it establishes equipment safety; those are broader claims requiring evidence beyond the fastener drawing.

#### Select the manufacturing route against the real order pattern

A small engineering batch and a repeat-production programme can justify different routes. Turning may be worth evaluating for an early geometry review or a complex combination of shoulders and holes. Cold heading may be appropriate for repeat volumes after the geometry and tooling scope are reviewed. A hybrid route can produce a formed blank and then finish selected functional features. None of these options is automatically the lowest-cost route simply because the application belongs to a growing industry.

Compare the whole programme rather than only a unit-price line. Separate tooling, sample quantities, secondary operations, surface treatment, inspection records and packaging. Identify which dimensions remain open during development and what a later change would require. A low initial part price can conceal a costly redesign if the interface is still moving. Conversely, retaining a flexible prototype route indefinitely can miss a sensible production opportunity. The route decision should be revisited after sample approval, using the expected repeat quantity and the final drawing.

#### An illustrative drawing-review exercise

Consider a removable charging-cabinet cover with a gasket and a threaded receiving insert. This is a design-review example, not a delivered ZUFEK customer case. The initial request specifies a flange screw and a security recess, but gives no section through the joint. Before quoting, the review team asks for the panel stack, gasket design condition, insert depth, access envelope and maintenance procedure. These questions are not delays added by manufacturing; they establish what the proposed part is supposed to achieve.

The section reveals that a shortened screw could reduce bottoming risk but also reduce usable engagement in the thickest panel condition. Enlarging the flange might improve coverage while interfering with an adjacent formed edge. Changing the recess could require a different service bit. There is no responsible universal answer from those observations alone. The team records each proposed change, obtains approval from the equipment designer, and then defines a sample check on the actual assembly. No torque, leak or corrosion result is assumed before the required evaluation is performed.

#### Build an acceptance plan that matches the failure modes

List the failure modes that matter for this interface: wrong thread, incomplete seating, insufficient clearance, an unusable drive, an incorrect finish or a mixed drawing revision. Then identify a suitable check for each. Dimensional measurements, thread gauges, matching-tool trials and assembly checks answer different questions. CCD vision may help assess accessible profiles and visible features, but a silhouette does not establish material strength, coating chemistry or a hidden seating condition. Those require their own appropriate methods and records.

Distinguish first-article approval from repeat-lot release. First-article review can establish whether the design and route produce an acceptable interface. Production release must then define what is checked, how results are recorded, which documents accompany the shipment and how lots remain identifiable. If every piece must be checked for a particular characteristic, name the characteristic and the method rather than writing an undefined “100% inspection” note. Inspection frequency, test scope and any destructive checks should be agreed with the purchaser for the actual risk and specification.

#### Ask better purchasing questions

Before comparing quotations, send the same drawing revision, assembly context, material condition and finish requirements to each supplier. Ask each to state assumptions, proposed routes and exceptions explicitly. Confirm whether tooling is dedicated, how sample changes are handled, what records are included and how a treatment change will be communicated. These questions make offers more comparable and reveal where an apparently equivalent quotation covers a different delivery condition.

Keep lead-time milestones separate. ZUFEK’s typical tooling and sampling discussion is approximately 10–15 days, subject to drawing review and confirmation; that is not an unconditional promise for every enclosure project. Material availability, special treatment and required verification can affect the agreed schedule. Repeat-production delivery is quoted separately. Define when the sampling clock starts, what the purchaser must approve and which open questions could stop progress. A realistic schedule has visible dependencies instead of an attractive number that nobody can connect to an approved specification.

#### A practical handover package

The handover should contain the controlled part drawing, a mating-interface reference, the approved sample status, the material and finish basis, the inspection plan and the packaging identification. Identify who can approve substitutions and which changes trigger a new review. If multiple cabinet variants share the part, list them under a controlled reference rather than assuming that an informal family name covers every version. This helps later purchasing teams understand why the approved geometry exists.

The strongest response to electrification demand is not to label ordinary parts with a new industry name. It is to make the connection between equipment function, manufacturable geometry and acceptance evidence explicit. When those links are visible, the buyer can discuss price and lead time with fewer hidden assumptions. When they are missing, a detailed-looking screw drawing can still leave the most important assembly decision unresolved. Start with the joint, preserve the approved interfaces, and make every proposed shortcut answerable against the actual equipment requirement.

#### Sources and scope

Source context is distinguished from ZUFEK editorial analysis. Examples are illustrative, not delivered customer cases or measured test results. Check the applicable current specifications for your product.

Industry Insights

### Factory automation: specifying locating and pivot fasteners for repeatable assemblies

A fastener in an automated fixture may do much more than hold two parts together. Its shoulder can locate a plate, its head can limit travel, or its shank can become the bearing surface for a moving element. Those functions make small dimensional relationships important, but “precision screw” is not a complete specification. A useful drawing explains which surfaces establish the assembly, what movement is intended and how the final condition will be checked. Without that information, a supplier can manufacture an attractive part that is dimensionally plausible yet wrong for the machine.

Theo Wan · 2026-10-30 Industry context without unsupported performance claims Separate locating, bearing and clamping functions Review both ends of the axial stack Specify the relationship between axes and surfaces Decide whether grinding is necessary from the requirement Match prototype flexibility to production economics A pivot-fixture review example Make tool access and adjustment repeatable Prevent spare-part confusion Build an inspection and release plan around function What a useful RFQ contains

#### Industry context without unsupported performance claims

IFR’s World Robotics reporting documents the deployment of industrial robots and the installed base of automation. That evidence supports discussing automation as a real manufacturing context. It does not tell a fastener supplier what tolerance to promise or prove that a particular fixture will remain accurate. This article does not extrapolate a robot-market statistic into a ZUFEK sales forecast. It examines the engineering and purchasing questions that arise when drawing-defined screws become parts of positioning, pivoting and adjustment interfaces.

As equipment platforms evolve, designers often want common spare parts and faster replacement. Those goals can conflict with informal customisation. Two shoulder screws can have the same nominal thread and overall length while locating from different faces, carrying different coatings or providing different usable bearing lengths. The difficulty is not merely making a small part accurately. It is maintaining a clearly defined relationship between the fastener, the mating components and the approved assembly procedure through design changes and repeat orders.

#### Separate locating, bearing and clamping functions

A locating surface establishes position. A bearing surface permits or supports movement. A clamping surface transfers a tightening load into the joint. One screw may contribute to several functions, but the drawing should identify them separately. If the threaded portion is intended only to retain the part, do not use its nominal axis as an unexamined substitute for the required locating datum. Conversely, a close-fitting shoulder does not automatically mean that every remaining diameter needs an equally tight tolerance.

Ask what would happen if each feature moved within its allowed limits. Would the mating plate shift, would a pivot bind, or would a cover simply remain clear? That review helps direct manufacturing effort toward the features that control function. It also helps the purchaser distinguish a functional requirement from a dimension copied from an older drawing. A short assembly explanation can be more valuable than adding another decimal place to every dimension. It gives the supplier a basis for asking useful questions rather than guessing which measurements the customer actually cares about.

#### Review both ends of the axial stack

For a pivoted cover, the shoulder must interact correctly with the complete thickness stack. Include washers, bushings, spacers, coatings and the actual seating face. At one extreme, the stack may be clamped before the intended shoulder seat is reached. At the other, the assembly may have more axial movement than intended. A nominal shoulder length between those two outcomes is not enough; the allowed variation of the mating parts must be considered alongside the screw’s variation.

Show where the shoulder length is measured from and which final surface condition applies. If a washer changes the contact plane, treat it as part of the controlled assembly. If a threaded receiving hole has limited depth, check bottoming separately from shoulder seating. These conditions can produce similar tightening sensations while representing different failures. The assembly review should identify the desired stop and the surfaces that must remain free. That information is needed before anyone can responsibly select a shoulder-length tolerance or recommend a change in the part.

#### Specify the relationship between axes and surfaces

A diameter tolerance controls size; it does not by itself control every relationship that affects motion. Where the assembly depends on the shoulder’s relationship to a thread, head face or another step, identify the relevant datum system and geometric requirement. Avoid a generic note such as “all concentric” without a defined basis and acceptance method. A drawing should allow both the manufacturer and the inspector to understand what is being constrained, in which setup and relative to which functional interface.

The inspection plan must then use methods appropriate to those requirements. A two-dimensional optical profile can show accessible lengths and diameters, but it does not establish every three-dimensional relationship. A thread gauge checks a different characteristic from a rotating functional trial. A mating-part check can expose an assembly problem while remaining insufficient to identify its dimensional cause. Using these methods together can be useful, but they are not interchangeable. Agree the evidence needed for the actual drawing instead of allowing the name of an instrument to stand in for an acceptance requirement.

#### Decide whether grinding is necessary from the requirement

Not every shoulder screw needs grinding, and grinding is not a substitute for a coherent drawing. The decision depends on the required final size, form, surface condition, material and process sequence. Turning may produce an acceptable interface for one application; another may require an additional finishing operation. A statement that a whole product family is always ground can hide unnecessary cost or conceal which surface is actually controlled. Ask which requirement makes the finishing operation necessary and when it is performed.

If heat treatment or coating follows a precision operation, review how the final delivered condition will be achieved and accepted. A measurement on an unfinished shoulder does not automatically establish the size after later processing. Identify any machining or treatment allowance and define the surfaces protected from, or included in, a finish. This is especially important where the drawing combines a locating shoulder with a threaded interface. The quote should describe the proposed route sufficiently to show how both interfaces will reach their agreed final state.

#### Match prototype flexibility to production economics

An early automation programme often contains unresolved assembly details. A turned prototype route may help evaluate multi-step geometry, holes or special head features without committing immediately to a production forming tool. Once the assembly is approved and repeat volumes are clearer, cold heading or a hybrid route may deserve review. The correct comparison includes tooling, secondary operations, final finishing and inspection, not simply the machining time of the first sample.

Document which design features are frozen before authorising tooling. A later change to a locating diameter may have a different consequence from a change to a non-functional head chamfer. Ask how proposed changes will be assessed and what evidence will be required after a route change. The purchaser should not assume that a production part is interchangeable merely because it was generated from the same nominal drawing on a different route. Equally, a supplier should not treat an approved prototype as permission to change a critical interface without review.

#### A pivot-fixture review example

Consider a small inspection fixture with a cover that rotates on a shoulder screw and stops against a separate feature. This is an illustrative engineering exercise, not a report of a customer delivery. The buyer initially asks for a tighter shoulder diameter because the cover feels loose. Reviewing the assembly shows that some movement comes from the mating bore, some from the axial stack and some from the way the cover is supported. Tightening only the screw diameter could reduce one clearance while leaving the actual instability unresolved.

The team therefore separates radial movement, axial movement and the desired stop function. It identifies the relevant bore and seat, records their drawing limits and defines how movement will be evaluated on a sample assembly. If a revised shoulder is proposed, the supplier receives the change through a controlled drawing revision. The example does not establish a universal clearance or torque value. Its lesson is that a functional complaint should be translated into measurable interface questions before it becomes an expensive tolerance change.

#### Make tool access and adjustment repeatable

Adjustment screws and knurled heads introduce a different set of questions. Will the operator use a hand grip, a hex key or a powered tool? Is the adjustment made once during setup or repeatedly during service? Can the operator approach the drive squarely, and does nearby equipment obstruct a larger head? A head-size change can affect access and operating feel even when the thread remains unchanged. These are assembly requirements, not decorative choices to be settled after manufacture.

If a locking method is required, state how the adjusted position will be retained and what verification is needed. Do not assume that a different thread pitch or a rougher surface will solve every movement problem. Pre-applied locking material, a separate locking element or another arrangement changes installation and service conditions. The equipment designer should define the required behaviour and approve the selected approach. The fastener supplier can then review the resulting geometry and processing requirements without being asked to infer the entire mechanism from an isolated component photograph.

#### Prevent spare-part confusion

Automation equipment can remain in service across several drawing revisions. A replacement part that looks correct may belong to another revision or assembly variant. Use a controlled part identifier and document which changes affect interchangeability. Lot labels should connect supplied parts to the applicable drawing and delivery condition. Where practical, packaging should help the customer keep variants separate during stores handling and line replenishment. A consistent label can prevent a problem that cannot be detected by casual visual comparison at the machine.

When a supplier proposes an alternative material, coating or manufacturing route for continuity of supply, review it as a controlled change. The change may affect more than strength or appearance. Surface condition, friction, final fit and service-tool compatibility can all matter to the equipment. Record the approved scope and any repeat checks rather than relying on an informal statement that the part is equivalent. This protects both parties: the buyer can trace the decision, and the supplier has a clear basis for what was accepted.

#### Build an inspection and release plan around function

List the dimensions and relationships that control locating, pivoting, adjustment and retention. For each, identify an inspection method, the delivery condition to be measured, the sampling or checking frequency and the record required. Separate material documentation, dimensional checks, thread acceptance and any assembly evaluation. A single certificate titled “inspection report” should not be treated as evidence for characteristics that were neither measured nor specified. If an external test is required, agree its scope and responsibility before placing the order.

First-article review should confirm both the loose part and the intended interface where necessary. Repeat-lot release should preserve the characteristics that made the sample acceptable. If a customer requires every part to be checked for a visible profile, define that profile and the sorting criteria. Do not extend that claim to hidden geometry or mechanical performance without the necessary method. This distinction makes inspection meaningful and prevents the phrase “full inspection” from becoming a substitute for an actual control plan.

#### What a useful RFQ contains

Provide the controlled screw drawing, relevant mating details, intended movement, quantity range, material and finish basis, critical characteristics and required records. Mark unresolved questions openly. Explain whether the request is for a flexible prototype route, a production proposal or a spare part that must remain interchangeable with existing equipment. Ask the supplier to identify route assumptions and exceptions, rather than accepting a quotation that silently interprets missing information.

Repeatable automation depends on defined interfaces and controlled changes, not on describing every small component as high precision. A buyer who can explain which surface locates, which surface moves and which surface clamps has already improved the manufacturing conversation. The next task is to connect those functions to dimensions, final processing and evidence. That is how a custom fastener becomes a dependable part of an equipment design: through an explicit, reviewable specification that survives the journey from first sample to replacement order.

#### Sources and scope
